We will explain the meaning of TTPs with an example of a Car \xe2\x80\xa2 Tactics - The employment and ordered arrangement of forces in relation to each other \xe2\x80\xa2 Preventative Maintenance \xe2\x80\xa2 Techniques - Non-prescriptive ways or methods used to perform missions, functions, or tasks \xe2\x80\xa2 Changing Oil \xe2\x80\xa2 Procedures - Standard, detailed steps that prescribe HOW Procedures \xe2\x80\xa2 In the detailed information of each technique specific examples or threats are included as available \xe2\x80\xa2 Not all procedures are included, but the data set is large and process to create meaningful hunt hypotheses 1) Identify the Tactic and Technique 2) Identify the Procedure(s) 3) Identify the Collection Requirements 4) Identify the Scope 5) Document Excluded Factors \xe2\x80\xa2 Intended to be used to create hunt hypotheses to be completed in one week Phase 1: Identify the Tactic & Technique \xe2\x80\xa2 High level what are you looking for? \xe2\x80\xa2 Used to track interest (tactics) over time in environment \xe2\x80\xa2 Attacks rarely use only one Tactic or Technique \xe2\x80\xa2 Specifically focus your efforts Phase 2: Identify the Procedures \xe2\x80\xa2 Specific examples and implementations of the selected technique \xe2\x80\xa2 Frequently found in APT reports, threat intelligence, etc. \xe2\x80\xa2 Understand and examine the different procedures \xe2\x80\xa2 What can and cannot be easily changed across all of the procedures? \xe2\x80\xa2 Perform research to understand the basic concepts of each procedure Phase 3: Identify Collection Requirements \xe2\x80\xa2 Bulk of the research time \xe2\x80\xa2 Replicate malicious activity in the lab \xe2\x80\xa2 Identify common behaviors \xe2\x80\xa2 Identify high false positives \xe2\x80\xa2 If possible, test in a small portion of the network \xe2\x80\xa2 Should result in a POC collection capability which gathers desired data Phase 4: Identify the Scope \xe2\x80\xa2 Two factors for scope: \xe2\x80\xa2 Time \xe2\x80\xa2 Length of execution window \xe2\x80\xa2 We recommend starting with week long execution windows \xe2\x80\xa2 Number of data sources to collect \xe2\x80\xa2 Can be host or network information \xe2\x80\xa2 How much data can be collected in the timeframe? \xe2\x80\xa2 How much data can be analyzed in the timeframe? \xe2\x80\xa2 Primarily based on collection requirements \xe2\x80\xa2 Scope may be limited due to limited collection capability Phase 5: Document Excluded Factors \xe2\x80\xa2 What things were you unable to include in the can manipulate their applied access token to access securable objects or perform privileged operations that they previously were not able to do. \xe2\x80\xa2 Procedures \xe2\x80\xa2 Token Impersonation (Theft) \xe2\x80\xa2 Create a Process with a Token \xe2\x80\xa2 Create Token \xe2\x86\x92 Impersonate Token https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1134 Windows Authentication Overview \xe2\x80\xa2 Windows creates a logon session upon successful authentication \xe2\x80\xa2 User credentials (if any) are stored in lsass.exe \xe2\x80\xa2 Credentials may be used later for Single Sign On \xe2\x80\xa2 Credentials are tied to the logon session \xe2\x80\xa2 Typical credentials: NTLM hash, Kerberos tickets, plaintext passwords \xe2\x80\xa2 Tokens define the security context of a process/thread \xe2\x80\xa2 When a process/thread wants to act in a user context it uses a token \xe2\x80\xa2 Interact with a securable object or perform an action that requires privilege \xe2\x80\xa2 Tokens are tied to logon sessions and determine how the cred is used Thread/Process \xe2\x86\x92 Token \xe2\x86\x92 Logon Session \xe2\x86\x92 Credential Logon Session Types \xe2\x80\xa2 The logon session type is the only thing that matters for credential/token theft \xe2\x80\xa2 NOT the token type. Credentials are tied to a logon session, NOT a token! \xe2\x80\xa2 Types \xe2\x80\xa2 Network logon (type 3): the client proves they have credentials, but does not send them to the server (credentials are NOT in memory) \xe2\x80\xa2 Non-Network logon (Interactive/NetworkCleartext/etc.): the client sends credentials to the service (credentials are in lsass.exe) \xe2\x80\xa2 Implication: \xe2\x80\xa2 If Logon Session Type is 3 (Network logon) then there is no credential/token to steal What is an Access Token? \xe2\x80\xa2 Kernel object that describes the security context of a process/thread \xe2\x80\xa2 Contains the following information: \xe2\x80\xa2 User Account Security Identifier (SID) \xe2\x80\xa2 Group SIDs \xe2\x80\xa2 Logon SID (Logon Session Identifier) \xe2\x80\xa2 List of Privileges held by user or groups \xe2\x80\xa2 Token Integrity Level \xe2\x80\xa2 Impersonation Level \xe2\x80\xa2 Optional list of restricting SIDs https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/aa374909(v=vs.85).aspx Token Types & Impersonation Levels \xe2\x80\xa2 1) Primary - a process token \xe2\x80\xa2 OS uses token\xe2\x80\x99s credentials to authenticate remotely. \xe2\x80\xa2 2) Impersonation - a thread token \xe2\x80\xa2 Threads use Impersonation tokens to impersonate other security contexts \xe2\x80\xa2 OS might use token\xe2\x80\x99s credentials to authenticate remotely \xe2\x80\xa2 Token Impersonation Levels \xe2\x80\xa2 Anonymous - Remote server cannot identify/impersonate client \xe2\x80\xa2 Identification - Remote server can identify user, but not impersonate \xe2\x80\xa2 Impersonation - The remote server can identify and impersonate the client across one computer boundary \xe2\x80\xa2 Delegation - The server can impersonate the client on across multiple boundaries, and can make calls on behalf of the client.
